title: A Rare Case of Coccidioidomycosis Meningitis
case_prompt:
A 46-year-old man with newly diagnosed coccidioidomycosis and HIV infection presented with 2 months of progressive shortness of breath, cough, pleuritic chest pain, diffuse joint pain, malaise, and intermittent fevers. He worked as a farmer in Bakersfield, California; he denied hemoptysis, recent travel, incarceration, or homelessness. Two weeks earlier he had tested positive for Coccidioides IgG.

On arrival he was tachycardic (133 bpm), tachypneic (RR 47), afebrile, normotensive, and hypoxic (SpO2 85% on room air). Examination showed coarse bilateral breath sounds, labored breathing, and 1–2-cm palpable subcutaneous nodules on both forearms. He was alert and oriented without neurologic deficits.

Chest CT with contrast revealed diffuse multifocal nodular consolidations and ground-glass opacities, a dense right upper-lobe consolidation, and prominent mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, without pulmonary embolism. Blood cultures were repeatedly negative. Tuberculosis testing was negative. Urine and bronchoalveolar lavage were negative for Histoplasma and Pneumocystis. Tests for Cryptococcus and Aspergillus were negative. Serum Coccidioides complement fixation titer was 1:64.

Lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 43 cm H2O, CSF glucose 81 mg/dL, protein 146 mg/dL, RBC 10 000/µL, WBC 4/µL, and Coccidioides IgG titer 1:1.

Noncontrast head CT showed a mass in the genu of the corpus callosum extending into the left lateral ventricle. Brain MRI without contrast demonstrated a 4.7 cm hemorrhagic mass involving the corpus callosum with surrounding edema.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered tuberculosis — “A differential diagnosis we considered on admission was TB. Given his immunocompromised state, appropriate testing for TB yielded negative results.”  
2. Considered histoplasmosis — “Patient was tested for histoplasmosis through urine studies and was found to be negative.”  
3. Considered Pneumocystis pneumonia — “In our patient, we did a bronchoalveolar lavage and pneumocystis was not found within the secretions.”  
4. Considered cryptococcal and aspergillus infection — “These were also considered in our immunocompromised patient; however, tests for both fungi were found to be negative.”  
5. Considered primary CNS lymphoma, glioblastoma, or cryptococcoma — “...it presented with features consistent with primary CNS lymphoma...could have also been a CNS lymphoma, glioblastoma or even a cryptococcoma.”  
6. Supported diagnosis of coccidioidal meningitis — “The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings of Coccidioides IgG antibodies were consistent with CM.”
